questions.q: Why would you use trim(upper(col("Borough"))) together in one expression?
options: To strip leading/trailing whitespace and force consistent casing in a single pass, since real data is rarely clean
trim() and upper() can never be combined in PySpark
To convert the column to a numeric type
To delete the Borough column entirely
questions.explain: Inconsistent whitespace and casing are exactly what breaks a join or groupBy later if left unaddressed.

questions.q: Why does concat(col("Zone"), lit(", "), col("Borough")) need lit() around the comma string?
options: A plain Python string can't be mixed directly into a column expression — lit() wraps it as a literal value Spark can place alongside real columns
lit() is only needed for numeric literals, never strings
concat() doesn't actually accept more than two arguments
lit() converts the string into a completely different column
questions.explain: Without lit(), Spark has no way to treat a bare Python string as part of the column expression.

questions.q: In substring(column, start, length), how is the start position indexed?
options: 1-indexed, not 0-indexed like Python's own string slicing
0-indexed, exactly like Python slicing
It varies depending on the column's data type
substring() doesn't take a start position at all
questions.explain: This trips up anyone coming straight from Python string handling, so it's worth noting deliberately.

questions.q: Where do functions like upper(), trim(), concat(), and substring() come from in PySpark?
options: pyspark.sql.functions — the same module col() and when() come from
They are built-in Python string methods, not PySpark functions at all
Each one requires a separate, differently-named import module
They only exist as methods directly on the SparkSession object
questions.explain: This is the single toolbox for building column expressions in PySpark — col(), when(), and every string function all live there.

questions.q: Why does inconsistent text formatting, like "queens" vs "Queens " vs "QUEENS", matter for later PySpark operations?
options: It can break a join or a groupBy later, since those operations typically match on exact string equality
PySpark automatically normalizes all text before any operation, so it never matters
It only matters for numeric columns, never text columns
Joins and groupBy operations ignore string values entirely
questions.explain: This is exactly why normalizing with trim()/upper()/lower() matters before Lessons 53 and 55's groupBy and joins.
